name: Alain Voge Cornas Les Vieilles Fontaines 2009
text:
## Alain Voge Cornas Les Vieilles Fontaines 2009

**The story.** Domaine Alain Voge is in [Cornas](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Cornas,+Ard%C3%A8che,+France&t=k), a small village in the Ardèche just north of Valence, in the northern Rhône. Alain Voge's great-grandfather Henri brought the family there in the early 20th century, when vines were just one part of a mixed farm. Alain, born in 1939, started working on the estate in 1961. When his father Louis died in 1965, he took charge alongside his mother.

Over the next decades Voge became one of the men who built Cornas's international name. He worked with a merchant to sell the wine in bottle rather than in bulk, and fought to protect the vineyards from the town's spread. He replanted the family's vines in the heart of Cornas (giving "Les Vieilles Vignes" in the 1970s) and brought the neighbouring white-wine appellation of Saint-Péray back to life. Decanter's Rhône expert Matt Walls said that leading one appellation is impressive, but leading two is rare.

In 2004 Albéric Mazoyer, previously a winemaker at Michel Chapoutier, joined as a partner and manager. Organic and then biodynamic certification followed; the estate says its vines and wine were certified organic from the 2016 vintage. Mazoyer handed over to Lionel Fraisse in October 2018. Alain Voge died in September 2020, aged 81.

**The vineyard: Les Vieilles Fontaines.** The name means "the old springs". In the locality called La Fontaine there is a spring that once supplied water to the house of a noble Cornas family. Voge first made this wine there in 1988, from the estate's oldest Syrah: about 0.9 hectares of vines now around 80 years old, on granite. It is made only in exceptional years; the estate lists 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 among the recent ones. Cornas is 100% Syrah by law.

**How it's made.** The estate's current sheet gives: Syrah vines trained as free-standing bushes on single stakes; hand-picked; partly destemmed, with about 30% whole bunches; wild-yeast fermentation and several weeks of maceration in steel vats, with daily punching-down and pumping-over; then 24 months in 228-litre Burgundy-size barrels, 15 to 20% of them new. Only about 2,400 bottles are made, and the estate gives it 25 years of ageing potential. (Details may have varied a little in older vintages.)

**Cornas itself.** The appellation is small: Wikipedia gives about 90 hectares, and the estate says 145 today. By comparison, some single Bordeaux châteaux are bigger than the whole of Cornas. The vines grow on steep, east- to south-east-facing slopes of granite and sandy, rocky soil. Cornas is sheltered from the mistral and is often the first northern Rhône appellation to harvest. Traditional Cornas was known as a tough, tannic wine needing 6 to 7 years before it was approachable.

**The vintage.** Jancis Robinson's northern Rhône vintage chart describes 2009 as warmer and drier than average. Volumes were down and the harvest was early. Ripening was quick but complete, and quality very good. She notes the reds are generally ageing well and should reach their peak in the 2020s. It was the first of two great years in a row: 2010, which followed, was hyped on release as possibly the best northern Rhône vintage in history, and the 2010 Vieilles Fontaines became the first Cornas to receive 100 points from Robert Parker.

**What the critics say for 2009.** Scores as listed by the London merchant Fine+Rare (checked on its page):
- **Wine Advocate: 97** (Jeb Dunnuck, September 2015, drink 2019 to 2039). He found it riper and more exuberant than the 2010: a hedonistic wine full of incense, flowers, black raspberries, toasted spices and violets; full-bodied, layered and "downright sexy", yet still classy, firming up on the finish. Hard to resist young, but with enough tannin for 4 to 5 more years in bottle (from 2015).
- **Vinous: 93+** (Josh Raynolds, March 2012, after bottling). Black and blue fruit preserves, candied licorice, strong vanilla and spice-cake notes; broad and juicy, then firmer, with youthful tannins. He suggested giving it a few years to absorb its oak. From barrel he had scored it 92 to 94.
- **Fine+Rare's average of the critics: 95.**
- **CellarTracker community: 92.6** (from your CellarTracker list).

The earlier note on this wine mentioned two 97s from critics. I could confirm one (Dunnuck's for Wine Advocate); I couldn't find a second.

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is seventeen years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2018 to 2038, and Dunnuck's runs to 2039. So it is right in the middle of its drinking years. In a ripe vintage like 2009 it should be generous and open now, the oak long absorbed, with dark fruit, flowers and spice joined by the savoury notes that come with age. Drink it any time over the next ten years or so.

**Serving.** At this age, stand the bottle upright for a day and decant gently to leave the sediment behind. Half an hour to an hour of air is plenty; older wines can fade if left open too long. Serve at 16 to 17°C in a large glass.

**Food.** Northern Rhône Syrah loves game and peppery, savoury dishes. My picks for this riper, softer vintage: roast venison or lamb, duck breast with cherries or a pepper sauce, beef braised in red wine, or wild mushrooms. Hard, aged cheeses work too. I'd avoid delicate fish and very spicy food.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists it, and the 2009 is now mostly found at auction and with fine-wine merchants such as Fine+Rare in London. At the domaine, the current 2023 vintage sells for €93, limited to three bottles per customer. For a 97-point Cornas with 17 years of age already on it, a bottle is a treat to own.

**From the history books**
- **"Burnt earth".** The name Cornas is Celtic and means "burnt earth", fitting for its sun-baked slopes. Wine from Cornas is mentioned in writing as early as 885 AD. It is said (though hard to prove) that Louis XV and Cardinal Richelieu both admired it.
- **A late starter in bottle.** Cornas became an official appellation in 1938, but local growers only began bottling their own wine around 1950. Until then most of it was sold in bulk. Pierre-Auguste Clape, who died in 2018 aged 93, began bottling his own Cornas in the 1950s, and Alain Voge belonged to the same pioneering generation that made Cornas known abroad.
- **Saving the slopes.** Voge spent the 1970s and 1980s replanting and regenerating old Cornas vineyard sites, and became a leading voice in protecting the vineyards from the spread of housing.
- **A first for Cornas.** In December 2012 Robert Parker gave the 2010 Vieilles Fontaines 100 points, the first perfect score for any Cornas. He called it one of the few perfect Cornas he had ever tasted.
- **Saint-Péray reborn.** Voge also pioneered barrel-fermented still white wines in neighbouring Saint-Péray in the 1980s and is credited with revitalising that appellation. The estate's Saint-Péray range includes one called "Les Bulles d'Alain" ("Alain's bubbles").

**Curious details**
- **A chef's pairing.** For this wine the estate suggests venison in sake lees, a dish created by chef Anne-Sophie Pic at her restaurant in nearby Valence.
- **Tiny production.** About 2,400 bottles a year, from less than one hectare, and only in great years.
- **Smaller than a château.** The whole Cornas appellation makes less wine than some single Bordeaux estates.
- **The spring is real.** The "fontaine" of the name is an actual spring in the La Fontaine locality, which once fed a noble family's house.
